chapters.title: Chapter 5: Costs, Margins, and Taxes of Hedging in India

lessons.title: SEBI's F&O Rules and What They Mean for Retail Hedgers

children.text: Almost every rule you have had to work around in this course, the large lot size, the full premium paid upfront, the Tuesday expiry, came from a single problem SEBI set out to fix: retail investors losing enormous sums speculating in index options. The regulator's response, starting with a circular on 1 October 2024, reshaped the derivatives market. None of it was aimed at hedgers, but all of it applies to them. This lesson goes through each change and asks one question every time: what does it mean for someone using options to protect a portfolio?

body.text: SEBI's derivatives reforms were written to slow down speculators. For hedgers, they raised the minimum size of a hedge, removed leverage from buying options, and pushed activity towards monthly contracts. Two of those three changes actually suit a hedger's way of working.

children.text: You met the numbers in Chapter 1. SEBI's study covering FY22 to FY24 found that 93% of individual traders in equity F&O lost money, with aggregate net losses of over ₹1.8 lakh crore. Weekly index options, where a contract could be bought and lost within hours, accounted for much of the activity. The reforms that followed were designed to raise the cost and seriousness of entry, not to ban anything.

body.title: The main changes and when they took effect

events.title: SEBI announces the framework
events.description: A circular sets out six measures to strengthen the equity index derivatives framework, to be phased in over the following months.

events.title: Bigger contracts, fewer weekly expiries
events.description: Minimum contract value for index derivatives rises from about ₹5 lakh to ₹15 lakh, exchanges revise lot sizes upwards, and each exchange is allowed weekly expiries on only one benchmark index. Extra margin is also applied on expiry day.

events.title: Full premium upfront
events.description: Brokers must collect the entire option premium from buyers upfront. The calendar spread margin benefit on expiry day is also removed.

events.title: Intraday position limit monitoring
events.description: Exchanges begin monitoring index derivatives position limits during the day rather than only at the end of it.

events.title: Expiry days standardised
events.description: SEBI restricts equity derivatives expiries to Tuesdays or Thursdays, one weekly day per exchange. NSE chose Tuesday and BSE chose Thursday.

events.title: Delta-based open interest
events.description: Position limits move to a delta-adjusted future equivalent measure, phased in over the following months. This mainly affects large and institutional participants.

children.text: What Each Rule Means for a Hedger

body.caption: The rules, translated into hedging terms

cells: Raised from about ₹5 lakh to ₹15 lakh, with lot sizes revised upwards
The biggest constraint. Portfolios below roughly ₹15 lakh of index exposure can no longer be hedged without a large over-hedge
Weekly contracts only on one benchmark index per exchange
Little impact. Hedgers use monthly or longer contracts, which are unaffected
Weekly and monthly expiries on Tuesday for NSE and Thursday for BSE
Administrative. Note the right day when planning rolls and reminders
Neutral to positive. A hedger pays the premium in full anyway, and it prevents accidental over-buying
Additional margin for short positions on expiry day
Only matters if you sell options, such as the short leg of a collar or a covered call
Intraday position limits and delta-based open interest
Exposure monitored during the day, measured in future equivalent terms

stats.label: Minimum index contract value
stats.context: Raised from about ₹5 lakh, effective 20 November 2024

stats.label: Weekly expiries per exchange
stats.context: Nifty 50 on NSE, Sensex on BSE

stats.label: NSE expiry day
stats.context: BSE uses Thursday. Monthly contracts expire in the last week of the month

body.text: Notice how well the reforms fit a hedger's habits, almost by accident. Weekly speculation got harder while monthly and longer contracts, the ones a hedger actually wants, were left alone. Buyers now pay in full, which is what a hedger does anyway. The one genuinely painful change is the contract size, and it hits exactly the investors this course keeps telling not to hedge: those with portfolios too small to match a single lot.

body.title: Who got priced out
body.prompt: Before the change, one index option contract had to be worth at least about ₹5 lakh. After it, the minimum is about ₹15 lakh. By how many times did the smallest possible hedge grow?
body.explanation: ₹15 lakh ÷ ₹5 lakh = 3. An investor with a ₹7 lakh portfolio could once buy a contract that roughly matched it. Today the smallest Nifty contract is more than twice their portfolio, so any hedge would be a leveraged bet on a fall rather than protection.

body.title: Mark your calendar
body.textWithBlank: Under the standardised expiry framework, NSE equity derivatives, including Nifty options, now expire on a ___.
body.explanation: SEBI limited expiries to Tuesdays or Thursdays, with one weekly day per exchange. NSE chose Tuesday and BSE chose Thursday. If expiry day is a holiday, it moves to the previous trading day.

children.text: The Rule That Can Remove Your Hedge Entirely

There is one more piece of regulation that hedgers of individual stocks need to watch. SEBI periodically revises the eligibility criteria for stocks in the derivatives segment, based on measures such as turnover and market width. Stocks that no longer meet the criteria are removed, and once existing contracts expire, there are no options on that stock at all. An investor who was relying on protective puts for a concentrated holding can find the tool simply gone.

body.title: Where the rules help hedgers and where they hurt

columns.label: Helps
points: Full premium upfront removes any chance of buying protection on borrowed money
Curbs on weekly speculation leave monthly and quarterly contracts, which hedgers prefer, untouched
Standard expiry days make rolling schedules easier to plan
Tighter risk monitoring supports the stability of the market a hedger depends on

columns.label: Hurts
points: Larger contracts put hedging out of reach for portfolios below roughly ₹15 lakh of exposure
Coarser lot sizes make it harder to land near your exact hedge ratio
Extra expiry-day margin raises the cost of any short leg, including collars
Stocks leaving the derivatives segment can remove single-stock protection altogether

body.title: Which change affects you most?
body.question: An investor holds ₹40 lakh in Nifty index funds and hedges twice a year with monthly Nifty puts, never selling options. Which of SEBI's changes has the greatest practical effect on them?
options: The extra margin on expiry day
Limiting weekly expiries to one benchmark index per exchange
Larger contract sizes, which change how many lots match their portfolio
body.explanation: They buy only, so margin rules do not touch them, and they do not use weekly contracts. Delta-based open interest matters at institutional scale. The larger lot size changes their hedge ratio arithmetic, which is the one thing they must recalculate.

body.title: The portfolio that fell below the minimum
body.scenario: Prakash, 44, runs a printing business in Ludhiana and has ₹11 lakh in Nifty 50 index funds. A few years ago he hedged before every Budget by buying one Nifty put that closely matched his portfolio. He tried to do the same this year and found that one lot now represents over ₹16 lakh, about 150% of his portfolio. He asks whether he should just buy the lot anyway, since the premium is only about ₹16,000.
body.prompt: What would you tell Prakash, and what alternatives does he have?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Buying one lot would leave him about 150% hedged. The extra half lot is a directional bet that the market will fall, not protection, and he should be clear that is what he is doing.
2. The cost is also higher than it looks. ₹16,000 is about 1.5% of his ₹11 lakh portfolio for a quarter of cover, and he would pay it before every Budget and every other event he worries about.
3. Alternative one, and usually the best: no hedge. A ₹11 lakh portfolio with a long horizon can absorb a correction, and the money saved on premium compounds.
4. Alternative two: if a specific goal is at risk, move that amount into a debt fund or an FD for the period. No premium, no basis risk, no lots.
5. Alternative three: if he genuinely needs event protection and accepts the over-hedge, he should size it deliberately, write down the exact amount of the excess, and treat that part as a speculative position with money he can lose.
The lesson: when the smallest available hedge is much larger than your exposure, the honest answer is usually that options are not the right tool for your portfolio yet.

body.title: Position limits and delta-based open interest, briefly

children.text: Exchanges cap how large a position any single participant can hold in a contract, so that nobody can dominate or distort it. Two recent changes tightened this. First, those limits are now monitored during the trading day rather than only at the close. Second, exposure is measured in future equivalent terms: options are converted using their delta, so that a large position in far out-of-the-money options counts for what it is actually worth in market risk rather than by contract count.

For a retail hedger holding two or three lots, neither change is noticeable. They matter to proprietary desks, foreign investors and large funds. The reason to know about them is simpler: they are part of why the market you hedge in is more closely supervised than it was, and they explain the jargon you will see in market commentary.

body.label: Rules change faster than courses
body.value: Check the source before every hedge
body.context: Lot sizes, expiry days, margins and eligibility lists are all set by circular. The NSE and SEBI websites are the only authoritative versions.

body.title: Stay on the right side of the rules
steps: Before each hedge, confirm the current lot size and the resulting notional value per lot on the NSE website.
Check the expiry calendar for the contract you are using, including any holiday shifts.
If your portfolio is below roughly one lot of exposure, decide deliberately between no hedge, reducing equity, or a knowingly over-sized position.
If you hedge a single stock, check that it is still in the derivatives segment before you rely on it again.
Skim SEBI and exchange circulars once a quarter, or follow a broker's updates page, so that rule changes do not surprise you mid-hedge.

body.label: SEBI Circulars
body.description: The official source for derivatives circulars, including the measures described in this lesson. Always prefer the circular to a news summary.

cards.definition: The smallest rupee value an index derivatives contract may have, raised from about ₹5 lakh to ₹15 lakh in November 2024.
Each exchange may offer weekly contracts on only one benchmark index.
Brokers must collect the full option premium from buyers before the trade, effective February 2025.
Equity derivatives expire on Tuesdays for NSE and Thursdays for BSE, under SEBI's May 2025 framework.
A delta-adjusted way of measuring positions, so exposure reflects real market risk rather than contract count.
The conditions a stock must meet to have derivatives. Stocks that fall short are removed, ending options on them.

points: SEBI's reforms followed evidence that most individual F&O traders lose money, and were aimed at speculation rather than hedging.
The minimum index contract value rose from about ₹5 lakh to about ₹15 lakh in November 2024, tripling the smallest possible hedge.
Weekly expiries are limited to one benchmark index per exchange, and NSE now expires on Tuesdays while BSE uses Thursdays.
Option buyers pay the full premium upfront, which changes nothing for a hedger but removes leverage from buying.
Extra expiry-day margin and intraday position monitoring mainly affect sellers and large participants.
Stocks can be removed from the derivatives segment, so single-stock protection is not permanently available.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Regulatory measures are summarised in plain language and may have been amended after this lesson was written. Effective dates and thresholds are as announced by SEBI and the exchanges, and the authoritative versions are the circulars themselves. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before acting.
